title: Mitotically heritable effects of BMAA on striatal neural stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
ehr_evidence: The study used primary striatal neurons and embryonic neural stem cells from rats (in vitro cell cultures) and pregnant outbred Wistar rats; no electronic or computerised health records were used.
summary: An in vitro/in vivo developmental neurotoxicology study using primary striatal neurons and embryonic neural stem cells from rats exposed to the cyanobacterial toxin BMAA, showing that neural stem cells are more susceptible than neurons to BMAA-induced reduced proliferation, increased apoptosis, impaired differentiation, and mitotically heritable morphological alterations.
key_findings: BMAA at 250 µM–3 mM reduced neural stem cell proliferation (decreased MTT production) and increased apoptosis and G2/M arrest, whereas primary striatal neurons were unaffected even at 3 mM.

At 50–100 µM, BMAA significantly reduced differentiation into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes (e.g., 100 µM BMAA reduced neurons from 31.72% to 16.66%, p<0.001; astrocytes from 34.38% to 15.49%, p<0.01; oligodendrocytes from 15.75% to 9.42%, p<0.05) while increasing undifferentiated cells.
BMAA-induced reductions in proliferation, differentiation, and neurite outgrowth were mitotically heritable to daughter cells (D1 and D2).
The NMDA antagonist MK-801 and metabotropic antagonist MCPG, but not the non-NMDA antagonist CNQX, completely protected against BMAA-induced effects on viability, proliferation, and morphology.
captured_features: Cell cycle phase distribution (G0/G1, G2/M) via flow cytometry
Differentiation marker expression (β III-tubulin, GFAP, oligo4, nestin) via immunocytochemistry and flow cytometry
Neurite length, processes per cell, branches per cell, and cell body area (morphometric analysis)
study_design: in vitro/in vivo experimental neurotoxicology study (cell culture and animal model)
data_source_type: biospecimen (rat striatal cell cultures and pregnant Wistar rats)
population: embryonic rat (Wistar) striatum at embryonic day 15/18; pregnant Wistar dams
limitations: In vitro/in vivo study using rat cells and animals; findings may not translate to humans
High micromolar-to-millimolar BMAA concentrations used that may exceed realistic human exposure
